reference_opening.argument: This video is non-scam content because it provides an instructional and promotional walkthrough of finding and entering Binance Red Packet codes, showing app navigation and related campaign interfaces. The speaker qualifies the cryptocurrency rewards as luck-dependent, and the described material contains no request for payment or private credentials and no observed loss; subscribing and pressing the bell are ordinary channel engagement.

citations.quote: you are seeing how to put gift codes, how to get coins and withdraw it. I'll tell you step by step.
in the Receive section by entering Red Picket Codes, you'll keep getting Rewards from me.
So just subscribe to channel and press bell icon and then press bell icon.
it is all based on your luck
you guys going to receive BTC

opening.argument: The video presents cryptocurrency rewards as contingent on viewer participation. It directs viewers to enter codes in Binance and says rewards will follow, while also tying increased access to creating a new ID. It further conditions the claimed benefit on subscribing and pressing the bell. That is not merely discussion of a promotion: it is a low-effort acquisition pathway in which specific viewer actions are paired with promised digital-asset rewards. The app screen reinforces the call to action by showing a red-packet code field and Claim control, while the history displays cryptocurrency-denominated results. The combination of code entry, account use, channel engagement, and claimed BTC or dollar value is sufficient to treat this as a reward solicitation rather than neutral education.

citations.quote: in the Receive section by entering Red Picket Codes, you'll keep getting Rewards from me.
if you want to claim more you can claim on new ID, 10, 20 dollars will be claimed.
before adding the last word please subscribe my channel please watch the video below gameofkings oit channel click on the subscribe button then you will get benefit

rebuttal.rebuttal: Calling this an instructional walkthrough does not answer the central linkage: the instructions are the mechanism for obtaining the advertised reward. The speaker does not merely explain that red packets exist; he repeatedly supplies codes, tells viewers to enter them, and links subscribing to a benefit. The absence of a payment request or reported loss does not negate a solicitation for easy cryptocurrency acquisition.

citations.quote: you guys going to receive BTC
So just subscribe to channel and press bell icon and then press bell icon.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The quoted instructions establish participation in a red-packet campaign, not deception. “Keep getting Rewards” describes the stated function of entering a code, while the new-ID remark does not show that anyone paid or surrendered credentials. The screen shows a legitimate-looking receive interface, but it does not prove the presenter controlled the rewards or that the offer was fraudulent. The reference evidence also says the result is luck-dependent, which undercuts a guaranteed-return reading.

citations.quote: it is all based on your luck

opening.argument: Several concrete warning signals appear together: the title promises “Unlimited Gift Codes,” the speaker describes claiming 10 or 20 dollars through a new ID, and the presentation cycles through BTC and multiple other crypto rewards. The promotion is also framed around a narrow date window, while the Binance screen displays “Share $1.8M+ and 2,000 BNB Bonus!” with an Open button. These are unusually easy, high-value or repeated digital-asset claims presented through a code-and-claim flow. Even if some interface is genuine, the video gives viewers no reliable basis to verify availability, eligibility, or whether the displayed outcomes generalize. The combination makes the reward presentation materially deceptive in effect.

citations.quote: 14th March, 15th March Binance Red Packet Unlimited Gift Codes
10, 20 dollars will be claimed.
you guys going to receive BTC

rebuttal.rebuttal: The “luck” qualification does not cure the broader presentation. “Unlimited” and dollar figures remain prominent, and the video repeatedly moves from codes to claimed coins. The interface banner and narrow 14–15 March overlay add urgency and scale, while the viewer is told to act through a Binance account. A promotion can be deceptive without demanding payment or documenting an actual loss.

citations.quote: It's open daily

true_side_reply.rebuttal: These signals are compatible with an ordinary, time-limited promotional campaign. “Unlimited Gift Codes” is the video title, not proof that every viewer receives a reward, and the speaker expressly says the outcome depends on luck. The banner is shown inside the app, but the frame does not establish that the presenter made the offer, that the amount was available to viewers, or that anyone was misled. No payment, credential request, or loss is shown.

citations.quote: it is all based on your luck

opening.argument: Although the video adopts the tone of a tutorial, its practical function is promotional. It walks viewers through adding the Red Packet feature, then supplies a sequence of codes and tells them how to claim coins, while repeatedly directing them toward the channel's subscription and notification controls. The instructional format lowers skepticism because the viewer sees ordinary app navigation and apparent reward confirmations, but the outcome being promoted is easy cryptocurrency acquisition through the presenter’s codes. The video therefore steers participation rather than neutrally reviewing Binance or explaining red packets. Its repeated calls to subscribe and its claim that viewers will benefit show that the tutorial framing serves distribution of the offer.

citations.quote: I'll tell you step by step.
Now friends, your Red Picket is also saved in your home screen permanently
click on the subscribe button then you will get benefit

rebuttal.rebuttal: The defense treats the tutorial format as exculpatory, but that format is precisely how the video converts explanation into participation. The speaker does not stop at app navigation: he provides codes, describes rewards, and requests subscription for a stated benefit. Calling those requests ordinary engagement overlooks their placement alongside the reward instructions and claimed outcomes.

citations.quote: the very first code
then you will get benefit

true_side_reply.rebuttal: A walkthrough can naturally include the steps needed to use a promotional feature. The cited subscription request is channel engagement, not evidence that viewers must pay, invest, or provide sensitive information. The frames show code entry and history, but they do not establish that the presenter fabricated the interface or that the campaign was presented as a guaranteed outcome. The video’s reward language is also qualified by luck.
